claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is homogeneous and single-phase.
The initial alloy has uniform grain-boundary composition.
The initial grain boundaries contain no detectable nanoscale precipitates.
Combined cyclic mechanical loading and elevated temperature drive localized grain-boundary segregation.
Localized grain-boundary segregation nucleates nanoscale intermetallic precipitates.
The nanoscale intermetallic precipitates trigger a transition to brittle behavior.
Cyclic stress and elevated temperature induce thermodynamically driven compositional fluctuations at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary compositional fluctuations promote nucleation of brittle intermetallic phases.
Brittle grain-boundary intermetallic phases serve as crack-initiation sites.
Crack initiation at the intermetallic phases impairs toughness.
Cyclically loaded, high-temperature samples will show more grain-boundary segregation than the baseline and controls.
Cyclically loaded, high-temperature samples will form nanoscale precipitates relative to the precipitate-free baseline and controls.
Cyclically loaded, high-temperature samples will exhibit a significant reduction in fracture toughness relative to the baseline and static controls.
The proposed brittle transformation is most pronounced under combined cyclic loading and elevated temperature.
Under static loading or sufficiently low temperature, the proposed brittle transformation may not occur.
The proposed segregation-and-precipitation-driven brittle behavior is unlike that seen in conventional alloys.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis characterizes the proposed behavior as unlike conventional alloys, but the stated mechanism—grain-boundary segregation followed by brittle intermetallic precipitation and crack initiation—is the same conventional-alloy expectation identified in the task context. No distinct high-entropy-alloy mechanism or contrasting conventional-alloy prediction is specified.
